title: Most simple axiom systems admit many different operator forms

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Most simple axiom systems admit many different operator forms

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Enumerating simple axiom systems for a binary operator shows that the vast majority allow operators of many different forms (many models), so they are not about any one particular operator and are far from complete; only a few, such as those for logic, force essentially a single form.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But what the pictures on the next two pages [804, 805] show is that the vast majority of axiom systems actually allow operators with all sorts of different forms.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), p. 803. Scope: simple equational axiom systems for a single binary operator

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-41: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.73

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The bounded enumeration behind the pictures can be reproduced with public model-finding software in weeks. Claims of unique form over unbounded models may require theorem proving, but the stated vast-majority computational observation is directly checkable under explicit search bounds.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate the stated bounded class of short binary-operator identities, use finite model finding and theorem proving to count non-isomorphic operator models, and compare the fraction with one versus many models. Alternative counts under the same bounds directly refute or confirm the observation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The bounds defining simple systems and model size must be specified.

The logic example depends on equivalence conventions.

Failure to find additional finite models does not prove uniqueness over all models.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The observation is a finite model-enumeration of the kind Mace4 performs, matching the book's tables for two, three, and four elements. A re-run either reproduces a strong majority of multi-model axioms or it does not. Infinite models are a further question; the claim as illustrated is about these finite operator forms, and that enumeration is feasible now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate short equational axioms for one binary operator and, with a finite-model finder, list the multiplication tables on two, three, and four elements that satisfy each axiom. The claim holds if, under an explicit simplicity ordering, most axioms admit many inequivalent tables and only a few force a single table.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite domains omit operators whose only distinguishing models are infinite.

Isomorphism pruning on three and four elements changes counts and leaves a qualitative majority meaningful.

Vast majority depends on the length cutoff and the ordering of axioms.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Among the simplest equational axiom systems for one binary operator (single equations with at most four operator occurrences), the large majority admit several non-isomorphic finite models (operator forms) on 2 and 3 elements, and only a small minority force a single form.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py enumerates all binary-tree term shapes with up to 4 operator occurrences split between the two sides, labels variables canonically (restricted-growth strings over the leaves of lhs then rhs), drops lhs == rhs and side-swapped duplicates (4692 systems), and for k = 2 and 3 evaluates every one of the 16 and 19,683 operator tables on every variable assignment with numpy, keeping the models and counting isomorphism classes via the canonical (minimal) table number over all permutations of the k elements. Validation family (lhs == a, up to 6 operators, k = 2 only) and the supplementary runs S1 (Wolfram's lhs == a family over {a, b} with up to 3 operators, k = 2, 3 exact plus a capped 4-element search) and S2 (capped 4-element search for the 2792 main-family systems not already 'many forms' at k = 3; --k4 flag, about 25 minutes) are described in interpretation and caveats. Default run about 2 minutes; derived/axioms.csv.gz (gzip, without the k2 model-set column) and derived/supplementary.json are from the --k4 run.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Family: all single-equation axiom systems lhs == rhs where lhs and rhs are terms built from one binary operator and variables, with a total of n = 1..4 operator occurrences in the equation, variables named canonically in order of first occurrence (a, b, c, ...) reading lhs then rhs, excluding equations with lhs identical to rhs, and identifying an equation with its side-swapped twin (so each unordered pair of sides is counted once). For each axiom system and each k in {2, 3}, enumerate all k^(k^2) operator tables (16 and 19,683), keep those satisfying the equation for every assignment of the variables, and count the models up to isomorphism (relabelling of the k elements by any permutation): m2 and m3. Definitions: 'many forms' = m3 >= 3; 'single form' = m2 <= 1 and m3 <= 1 and m2 + m3 >= 1; 'no non-trivial form' = m2 = m3 = 0 (only the one-element model). The claim PASSES if the fraction of axiom systems with 'many forms' is >= 0.80 and the fraction with 'single form' is <= 0.05. Reported, not decisive: the same fractions restricted to n = 4; the list of 'single form' systems; the systems whose k = 2 model set is exactly {Nand, Nor} (operators 7 and 1 in Wolfram's numbering) or {Xor, Xnor} (6 and 9); and, as a validation of the model-finding code against the note 'Properties of operators from axioms' (p. 1171), the k = 2 model sets of all lhs == a systems with up to 6 operators under this canonical labelling, listing how many allow only {6, 9} and only {1, 7} (the note reports 32,004 and 964 for its family of 274,499 systems; the family definition in the note is not fully specified, so this is a plausibility check, not a decisive comparison).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if fewer than 50% of the axiom systems have 'many forms', or if more than 20% force a 'single form'. Between those bounds and the pass thresholds the verdict is 'mixed'. If the enumeration cannot be completed for k = 3 within the run-time budget the verdict is inconclusive (underpowered).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of axiom systems with >= 3 non-isomorphic 3-element models ('many forms')

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: exhaustive enumeration, no sampling; 1900 of 4692 systems

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Wolfram's pictures (pp. 804-805) show, for a sequence of simple axiom systems, the operator forms (multiplication tables) allowed with 2, 3 and 4 elements, inequivalent under relabelling; his claim is that the vast majority of systems allow many forms and are 'not really about operators of any particular form', while a few (logic, i.e. Nand; junctional, equivalential and implicational calculi) force essentially a single form. This test reproduces that model enumeration for k = 2 and 3 only (k = 4 would require 4^16 tables per axiom, beyond the budget) over an explicit, exhaustively enumerated family of the simplest single-equation systems. 'Vast majority' is read as >= 80%, 'only a few' as <= 5%. Multi-axiom systems (e.g. group theory) are outside the enumerated family and are not needed for the majority statement.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: All single-equation axiom systems for one binary operator with 1-4 operator occurrences, canonical variable labelling (generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Pre-registered decision: 40.5% of the 4692 simplest single-equation axiom systems have 'many forms' (>= 3 non-isomorphic 3-element models), below the pre-registered 50% failure bound, so the 'vast majority' reading fails in this family; the 'single form' fraction (14.5%) falls in the mixed band (5-20%). The verdict follows the pre-registration, but the confidence is low because the result is sensitive to definitional choices listed below.

32.5% of the systems (1525) have no 2- or 3-element model at all (e.g. a o b == c, a o (b o c) == b o (a o c) == ... forcing a one-element structure); whether such degenerate equations belong to the population Wolfram had in mind is unclear. Excluding them, and adding a capped 4-element search (supplementary S2: 306 further systems gain >= 3 forms at k = 4; 1703 searches hit the node budget, so this is a lower bound), the many-forms fraction is 52.0% and the single-form fraction 6.4%, i.e. the mixed band rather than failure.

In Wolfram's own illustrated family (lhs == a with lhs over {a, b}, up to 3 operators; supplementary S1, 101 systems), 67 (66%) allow >= 3 forms for some k <= 4, 4 force a single form and 4 have no non-trivial form, which is closer to his description but still short of 'vast majority' at the 80% reading. The pre-registered validation against the note on p. 1171 was uninformative: under this canonical labelling no lhs == a system with <= 6 operators has k = 2 models exactly {Xor, Xnor} or {Nand, Nor}, because the note's family evidently uses a different variable convention (its counts 32,004 and 964 could not be reproduced).

Only models with 2 and 3 elements (and a capped 4-element search) were examined; the pictures in the book go to 4 elements exactly. Isomorphism is relabelling of elements only (duality/anti-isomorphism not identified). Thresholds (80% / 50%, 5% / 20%) are readings of 'vast majority' and 'only a few'. Six systems have exactly {Nand, Nor} as 2-element models, e.g. ((a o b) o (b o (a o a))) == b, consistent with the book's statement that short axioms for Nand exist, and 40 have exactly {Xor, Xnor}.
